title: Observing the unpredictable
caption: The BlackGEM telescopes under the Milky Way, La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: An unusual-looking telescope stands under a star-filled sky with the Milky Way in this view from ESO’s La Silla Observatory in Chile. It is BlackGEM, one of three telescopes ESO hosts at La Silla, a joint project of research institutes in the Netherlands and Belgium that can be operated remotely from Radboud University.

Violent events, such as mergers of neutron stars and black holes, send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves. Detectors like LIGO and Virgo can sense them but struggle to tell exactly where in the sky they came from. BlackGEM is built to find the visible light from such events, quickly.

Two black holes merging are “almost invisible.” But if at least one of the pair is a neutron star, some of its material escapes being swallowed, heats up and glows faintly. Once BlackGEM spots that glow, larger telescopes such as ESO’s Very Large Telescope can follow up in detail.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph credited to J. Rodrigues/ESO. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed here than it would to someone standing on site.

explore: BlackGEM’s name comes from its job: hunting the visible “counterparts” of gravitational-wave events, often caused by black holes. Its telescopes are designed for fast, wide searches of the sky.
alt: A compact, unusually shaped telescope under a starry sky with the Milky Way rising above it.
